title: Could you not watch one hour (Matthew 26:40)
hookLine: a holy hour answers his question in Gethsemane

cards: Late at night, in a garden of olive trees outside Jerusalem. Jesus has brought his three closest friends, Peter, James and John, and asked them one thing: stay awake with me.
He goes a little way off, falls on his face, and prays in anguish. When he comes back, they're asleep. Staying up with a sick child or a grieving friend goes like that.
The eyes just close. And Jesus says something to Peter that the Church still repeats.

teach.h: COULD YOU NOT WATCH ONE HOUR?
teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims: "What? Could you not watch one hour with me?" Some readers hear no anger in it, only disappointment, even tenderness. He goes on: watch ye, and pray, that ye enter not into temptation.
The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.
The Greek word for watch there is gregoreo: stay awake, keep alert, be on guard. The name Gregory is usually traced to the same root: the watchful one.
A holy hour is exactly what it sounds like: an hour spent in prayer, usually before the Eucharist in a church or chapel, often in adoration before the monstrance.
Catholics who keep one see it as answering that question with a yes.

Its modern form is often traced to Margaret Mary Alacoque, a French nun in the 1670s, who said Jesus asked her to spend an hour on Thursday nights keeping him company in his agony. The practice spread.
Fulton Sheen, the American bishop well-known on early television, made a holy hour every day of his priesthood and said it was the secret of whatever good he did.
Some parishes now have adoration chapels where someone signs up for each hour, so that day and night, someone is always watching.

What do you do for an hour? Pray, read Scripture, say a rosary, write, sit in silence, or simply look, like yesterday's farmer. Some who keep the hour say the start is the hardest, and then something settles.
And if an hour is too much, Catholics would say: start with less. The point is to stay awake with him.

how: Some Catholics make a holy hour, an hour of prayer before the Eucharist in a church or adoration chapel, often weekly on a set day, and some parishes keep adoration around the clock with sign-up hours.

games.q: you're Peter in the garden. you promised to stay awake. your eyes are closing. what happens?
o: you fall asleep, and he finds you.
games.why: they slept. he came back and said: What? Could you not watch one hour with me? the holy hour is an answer to that question.

practice: Put your phone in another room, or face down out of reach, and for the time the bell gives you, do nothing else: just stay awake, and stay here. Notice how often your hand wants to reach for something, and let it rest.
If you pray, think of Jesus in the garden and simply keep him company; if you don't, keep company with the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Holy hour. An hour of prayer, often before the Eucharist, answering Jesus's question in the garden: could you not watch one hour? Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to stay awake, keep watch. The word in Matthew 26:40–41, and the root of the name Gregory.

carryVoice: Your line: watch one hour. That was the week: the door, contrition, absolution, the seal, the tabernacle, the monstrance, and the holy hour. Day one hundred forty, done.
